text: Carbon dioxide makes up about 420 parts per million of Earth's atmosphere.
as_written: Because carbon dioxide makes up about four hundred and twenty parts per million of the atmosphere
source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Trends in Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide (2024)

text: Typical concrete contains about fifty percent oxygen by mass.
as_written: By weight, typical cured concrete is about fifty percent oxygen.
source: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Composition of Ordinary Concrete and Minerals

text: Oxygen makes up 20.95 percent of Earth's atmosphere by volume.
as_written: Because oxygen makes up twenty point nine five percent of the atmosphere by volume

text: Earth's total atmospheric mass is approximately 5 quadrillion metric tons (5.15 x 10^18 kg).
as_written: Earth has roughly five quadrillion metric tons of air pushing down on it.
source: National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), Trenberth et al., The Mass of the Atmosphere (2005)

text: Standard atmospheric pressure at sea level is 101.3 kilopascals.
as_written: At sea level, that pressure is one hundred and one point three kilopascals.
source: International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) Standard Temperature and Pressure

text: A 21 percent drop from 101.3 kPa leaves approximately 80 kPa.
as_written: The air drops from one hundred and one kilopascals to roughly eighty kilopascals.

text: The human tympanic membrane can rupture at a sudden overpressure or differential around 35 kilopascals.
as_written: The tympanic membrane inside your ears can rupture when exposed to a sudden differential of around thirty-five kilopascals.
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / NIOSH, Explosions and Blast Injuries: Eardrum Rupture Thresholds

text: Earth's continental crust is 46.6 percent oxygen by mass.
as_written: By mass, the continental crust is forty-six point six percent oxygen.
source: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), Abundance of Elements in the Earth's Crust

text: The ozone layer is concentrated between 15 and 35 kilometers above Earth's surface.
as_written: It resides in the stratosphere between fifteen and thirty-five kilometers above the surface
source: World Meteorological Organization (WMO), Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion

text: The ozone layer absorbs approximately 98 percent of medium-frequency UV light.
as_written: absorbing roughly ninety-eight percent of the sun medium-frequency ultraviolet light.
source: NASA Ozone Watch / NOAA Earth System Research Laboratories

text: Water is 88.8 percent oxygen by mass.
as_written: By mass, oxygen accounts for eighty-eight point eight percent of every water molecule.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Molecular Weight of Water Components

text: The human body is approximately 65 percent oxygen by mass.
as_written: The human body is roughly sixty-five percent oxygen by mass.
source: International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP), Report of the Task Group on Reference Man

text: Hydrogen gas has a flammability limit in air between 4 percent and 75 percent by volume.
as_written: Hydrogen can ignite in air at concentrations anywhere between four percent and seventy-five percent by volume.
source: National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 2, Hydrogen Technologies Code

text: The minimum ignition energy of a hydrogen-air mixture is approximately 0.02 millijoules.
as_written: The energy required to ignite a hydrogen-air mixture is minute, as little as zero point zero two millijoules
source: NASA Glenn Research Center, Safety Standard for Hydrogen and Hydrogen Systems (NASA-STD-8719.16)

text: The autoignition temperature of hydrogen gas in air is 536 degrees Celsius.
as_written: autoignition temperature of hydrogen, which is five hundred and thirty-six degrees Celsius.
source: U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Alternative Fuels Data Center, Hydrogen Properties

text: The enthalpy of formation of liquid water from gaseous hydrogen and oxygen is -285.8 kJ/mol.
as_written: The chemical reaction releases two hundred and eighty-six kilojoules of energy for every single mole of water formed.
source: NIST Chemistry WebBook, Standard Enthalpy of Formation for H2O(l)
